atlas-ae.0001: Two financial centres a hundred kilometres apart: Dubai, with the region’s largest regulated finance community and its main tech district, and Abu Dhabi, home to the sovereign funds and a fast-growing asset-management and AI scene. Graduate schemes at the biggest employers are for UAE nationals; Europeans usually enter through open roles or transfers.
atlas-ae.0006: UAE visas, residency rules, MoHRE contracts, Green and Golden visas and student routes are fully verified in visas_immigration/uae/uae_visas_immigration_guide.md.
atlas-ae.0007: No employer-stated entry pay for expatriate graduates was found; the only pay evidence is a recruiter’s guide saying most positions pay AED 10,000 to 40,000 a month.
atlas-ae.0008: The Italian foreign ministry’s travel advice (Viaggiare Sicuri) could not be read; only the UK’s is cited.
atlas-ae.0009: The UAE’s agreement with the EU does not cover Swiss, Norwegian, Icelandic or Irish citizens; their entry rules are not covered here.
atlas-ae.0010: Metrics are for the emirates, not the cities: Dubai’s GDP is at constant prices and Abu Dhabi’s is the published rounded figure; no average pay or rent figure from an official source was found, so neither is shown.
atlas-ae.0011: The Startup Genome ranks for Dubai and Abu Dhabi are reported through news sites for the global list (Dubai 12th and Abu Dhabi 41–50 among emerging ecosystems); the regional ranks come from Startup Genome’s own page.
atlas-ae.0012: Economics, accounting, management, marketing, analytics, data science and big data are not rated: no source read measures them by emirate.

atlas-ae.0021: Google, Oracle, SAP, Amazon, IBM among 4,000 companies
atlas-ae.0023: airline group headquartered in Dubai; Fortune Global 500 rank 474
atlas-ae.0024: 30,000 employees; graduate programmes presented for UAE nationals
atlas-ae.0027: Sovereign wealth, asset managers and an AI start-up push
atlas-ae.0030: 347 financial institutions, 171 asset and fund managers
atlas-ae.0033: real GDP of about AED 1.2 trillion in 2024, 54.7% non-oil
atlas-ae.0036: The best-known graduate programmes — ADIA, Mubadala, Emirates NBD, FAB and ADNOC — are for UAE nationals; non-nationals are mostly hired as experienced staff or transfers.
atlas-ae.0037: Private firms with 50 or more staff must add 2% Emiratis in skilled jobs each year; from 1 July 2026 each unfilled position costs AED 10,000 a month.
atlas-ae.0038: The UAE levies no income tax on individuals; VAT is 5%.
atlas-ae.0039: Italians who move without registering with AIRE are presumed to remain Italian tax residents; for the UAE, registering may not be enough without proof that your life has moved.
atlas-ae.0040: The UK Foreign Office reports strikes and retaliatory attacks by Iran in the region since 8 July 2026 and warns of flight cancellations and airspace closures; it does not advise against travel to the UAE as a whole.
atlas-ae.0041: Dubai International Financial Centre counts 1,052 regulated firms — over 290 banks and capital-markets firms, 135 insurers and over 500 wealth and asset managers — and a workforce of 50,200 at the end of 2025.
atlas-ae.0042: DIFC also hosts 1,677 AI, fintech and innovation companies, up 35% in 2025.
atlas-ae.0043: Dubai Internet City has about 4,000 companies and more than 31,000 professionals, among them Oracle, SAP, Amazon, Google, IBM and Cisco, and generates 65% of Dubai’s technology-sector output.
atlas-ae.0044: Jebel Ali handled 15.5 million TEU in 2024, its highest since 2015; DP World calls it the region’s leading trade and logistics hub.
atlas-ae.0045: Abu Dhabi Global Market had 347 financial institutions, 171 asset and fund managers and a workforce of 44,339 at the end of 2025, up by more than half in a year.
atlas-ae.0046: Abu Dhabi’s Hub71 counts 390 start-ups that have raised more than US$2.7 billion, with dedicated programmes for AI, climate tech, digital assets and life sciences.
atlas-ae.0047: The Global Financial Centres Index 40 (September 2026) ranks Dubai 9th of 117 financial centres (7th in the March 2026 edition) and first in the Middle East and Africa, and Abu Dhabi 13th (21st in March) and second, ahead of Casablanca (38th), Riyadh (46th), Doha (52nd) and Kuwait City (60th).
atlas-ae.0048: Startup Genome’s July 2026 report on the Middle East and North Africa ranks Tel Aviv first, Dubai second (ecosystem value US$30 billion, US$1.14 billion of Series A funding), Riyadh third and Abu Dhabi fourth (US$73 billion, with an AI-native ecosystem value of US$5.4 billion), and Doha eighth.
atlas-ae.0049: Reports on Startup Genome’s 2026 global ranking say Dubai is 12th among the top 100 emerging ecosystems, level with Riyadh at four unicorns, and Abu Dhabi has moved into the 41–50 band, up from 51–60.
atlas-ae.0050: Dubai’s GDP was AED 442.9 billion at constant prices in 2024 (AED 540.7 billion at current prices, up 5.8%), and its population reached 4,248,200 by the end of 2024.
atlas-ae.0051: Dubai’s economy produced about AED 355 billion in the first nine months of 2025, up 4.7%; financial and insurance activities were worth AED 42.8 billion, 12% of GDP.
atlas-ae.0052: Abu Dhabi’s real GDP reached AED 1.2 trillion in 2024, up 3.8%; non-oil activities made AED 644.3 billion, a record 54.7% of the total.
atlas-ae.0053: Abu Dhabi’s population grew 7.5% in 2024 to 4,135,985 people, 51% more than in 2014.
atlas-ae.0054: Fortune’s 2026 Global 500 lists the Emirates Group at rank 474, headquartered in Dubai, with 130,919 employees.
atlas-ae.0055: Emirates NBD’s careers page counts 30,000 employees and presents its graduate programmes within its Emiratisation offer for UAE nationals.
atlas-ae.0056: In Michael Page’s UAE Salary Guide 2026, more than 60% of the positions pay between AED 10,000 and AED 40,000 a month, and technology, digital, finance and accounting make up a third of them.
atlas-ae.0057: In a SkillDrift analysis of 7,025 UAE job postings, English was named in 21.3% and Arabic in 7.4% (13.2% in Saudi Arabia and 13.5% in Qatar), on a sample weighted to operations, engineering, sales and hospitality; the statutory job offer is issued in Arabic and English plus a third language the worker understands.
atlas-ae.0058: Graduate intakes are staggered rather than national: PwC Middle East’s assurance graduate programme starts in September 2026 and its summer internship runs from June to August 2026; Dubai Business Associates, a nine-month programme open worldwide, closed applications on 1 March 2026 for a September start; Emirates NBD takes one Ruwad cohort a year and Bedaya graduates at several points in the year; ADIA runs two cycles for UAE nationals, with applications due before 1 February and before 6 July.
atlas-ae.0059: The Federal Competitiveness and Statistics Centre reports UAE unemployment of 1.9% in 2024 (2.1% in 2023) and youth unemployment, ages 15 to 24, of 5.2% (16.7% in 2023); Khaleej Times quoted employers in June 2026 saying internships, project portfolios and certifications have become the minimum for entry-level roles.
atlas-ae.0060: The UAE runs a two-tier market. The prestigious graduate programmes, at the sovereign funds, ADNOC and the large banks, are reserved for Emirati nationals; foreigners are mostly hired as experienced staff, as transfers within a firm, or through a smaller number of open programmes, chiefly at the Big Four.
atlas-ae.0061: Hiring from abroad is routine: the employer sends a signed offer to the worker, applies for the work permit, and the worker enters on its approval.
atlas-ae.0062: Experienced-hire openings through recruiters and job portals
atlas-ae.0063: Non-nationals are mostly hired into the same firms as experienced staff, so most open expatriate roles ask for prior experience; a recruiter or portal posting is the usual first contact.
atlas-ae.0064: The employer can send the offer to a candidate abroad directly, through a recruitment agency or through a designated entity.
atlas-ae.0066: A first job at a firm’s European office followed by a move to Dubai or Abu Dhabi is the most common way a European graduate ends up in the Gulf.
atlas-ae.0067: The library’s review of employers’ pages finds intra-firm transfers one of the three channels open to non-nationals, with experienced hires and the few open programmes.
atlas-ae.0069: Some Big Four graduate programmes in Dubai are open to non-nationals, with sponsorship possible; the national programmes at ADIA, Mubadala, Emirates NBD and ADNOC are not.
atlas-ae.0070: PwC Middle East runs graduate programmes in assurance, consulting, deals and tax across 12 countries of the region, for a September start, asking for a GPA of 3.0 and a major in accounting, finance or business.
atlas-ae.0071: Dubai Business Associates, funded by the Dubai government, is the clearest programme open worldwide: 35 places from over 6,600 applicants in the last edition.
atlas-ae.0073: PwC Middle East’s summer internship ran for two months, June to August 2026, for students majoring in accounting, finance or business with a GPA of 3.0 or above.
atlas-ae.0074: Emirates NBD’s internships are for UAE national undergraduates, so a bank internship is not open to a foreign student.
